Im not sold on AI as a tool for a few reasons. One being how the models are trained. If they were trained to be optimized for best answers and accurate, that would be fine. But that isnt how a lot of public models are being designed. There is political chicanery often baked into the models to exclude data that the owners would not find aligned with their beliefs. The second is the impact on intellect. In the hands of a smart person with a thoughtful approach, it cam be a powerful tool to streamline work. But in the hands of the average person, who only wants things now, it will gut critical thinking and even basic skills in favor of ease. Why learn to read or write if things can be dictated at you or for you? Maybe that's to low hanging fruit. Why learn to compose, draw/paint, or create works of art if you can just prompt an aI to give you something that's "good enough". Outsourcing creativity and culture to a machine I dont beleive is going to have positive long term results. Not to mention that AI in the creative space incentives people to not even try and learn. Why bother when a prompt will generate 100s of images in the time you took to make one, flooding internet real-estate and people's attention with an avalanche of images. Why learn to correct or adjust a work if yiu can prompt AI to finish it for you. Or deep fakes. That will be a fun thing to tackle when governments, politicos, and other malicious actors create falsehoods to sway a population to react a certain way. There's places it can be useful. I just dont think its good for human consumption in the format its used now.

A lot of folks don't seem to get the difference between the general direction of history and mankind (which is what this video is right on about) and the day-to-day experience ("my coworker was replaced by AI"). Yes, there will be fluctuations along the way: CEOs who don't understand what AI is and what it can't replace, enthusiasts throwing way more at AI than is reasonable, others insisting on doing tasks by hand when they don't need to anymore, and so on. All these will make for different experiences we each go through, but won't alter the global course. Eventually things settle down, people who don't "get it" either adapt or fail and are replaced, and everything moves forward. Excellent video.

Spreadsheets didn't just impact accounting, but engineering. I was working in the nuclear industry in the early '80's for one of the power plant design companies. One of the things the group I worked in did was to calculate the radioactive isotope inventory for various components, in various scenarios. This included what would be put into containment for various accident scenarios. We had programs to do that calculation, but due to the limits of computers back then, the calculations for the accident scenarios were limited to specific time slices: Immediate, 1 hour, 10 hours, 100 hours, etc. The inventory of any given radionuclide was assumed to remain constant between any given time slice. This was inaccurate, since, depending on the decay rate for any given radionuclide, it could "disappear" between any one of those time slices. Tweaking the program we used to change the time slices was not a simple operation due to the nature of the code. When our department, yes department, got it's first PC, I created a spreadsheet in Lotus123 to do these calculations. I set up a row, where one column had the decay rate, and subsequent columns had the decay calculation for a time interval that was a variable from another cell. I copied that across multiple columns, and when I had the row set up, copies the whole row down the rest of the table. I then went in and updated each row for the appropriate decay rate for any given radionuclide, and I now had a spread sheet that could do the calculation for any time itnerval of interest by simply changing the value in the appropriate cell.
